title: How Kyle Corbin-Vasik Doesn't Dodge Bullets
body:
# How Kyle Corbin-Vasik Doesn't Dodge Bullets

## The Misconception

No one dodges bullets. A 9mm round travels at 370 meters per second. At engagement distance — call it ten meters — the bullet arrives in 27 milliseconds. Human visual processing takes 150 milliseconds minimum. The bullet hits you before your brain finishes registering the muzzle flash. This is physics. This is not negotiable. Not by augmentation, not by reflexes, not by anything short of prescience.

Kyle does not dodge bullets.

Kyle is not in the path of the bullet when it arrives.

## What the NeoCortex Array Actually Does

The experimental NeoCortex Program Atlas array — 32,768 electrodes, 256 threads, roughly 8x the density of standard Tier 3 corpo implants — gives Kyle two capabilities that, combined, produce what witnesses describe as "dodging bullets." Neither capability involves moving faster than a bullet.

### 1. Predictive Trajectory Rendering

Kyle's optic nerve threads interface with the NeoCortex array's spatial processing subsystem. In combat, this subsystem performs real-time ballistic analysis on every weapon in his visual field. The system identifies firearms by shape, estimates barrel orientation from grip angle and stance geometry, and renders augmented-reality trajectory lines — bright lateral lines extending from the barrel's bore axis to its intersection point with Kyle's body or the environment behind him.

These lines are not holograms. They are not projected. They exist only in Kyle's visual cortex, painted directly onto his perception by the electrode array. He sees them the way you see afterimages when you close your eyes — they are part of his vision, indistinguishable from reality. The lines update at the array's refresh rate: approximately 4,000 times per second. Faster than any display technology. Faster than conscious thought.

When an attacker's barrel is pointed at Kyle's center mass, he sees a red line connecting the barrel to his chest. When the attacker adjusts aim, the line moves. When Kyle moves, the intersection point moves. He can see, in real time, exactly where every gun in the room is pointed and exactly where those rounds will go.

### 2. Temporal Perception Dilation

The second capability is more dangerous and more expensive.

The NeoCortex array can accelerate Kyle's subjective perception of time. Not by speeding up his muscles — his body moves at normal human speed. By speeding up his brain. The array overclocks his neural processing, flooding his synapses with artificially accelerated signal propagation. The effect is that the world appears to slow down. Not metaphorically. Literally. His subjective experience of one second stretches to three, five, or — at maximum dilation — approximately eight subjective seconds per real second.

During temporal dilation, Kyle's brain is consuming glucose at a catastrophic rate. Standard human brain metabolism burns approximately 20 watts at rest. During full dilation, Kyle's brain metabolism spikes to an estimated 120-160 watts. The caloric cost is staggering — a three-second burst of full dilation burns roughly 1,200 calories. A sustained ten-second engagement at moderate dilation can cost 3,000-4,000 calories. This is why Kyle eats constantly. This is why he carries glucose tabs. This is why Mrs. Chen feeds him. His body is not sustaining a soldier. It is sustaining a furnace.

The side effects of dilation are cumulative and degenerative. Each use causes micro-hemorrhaging in the capillary beds surrounding the electrode array. The hemorrhages heal, but scar tissue accumulates. The scar tissue degrades signal quality. Degraded signal quality means the array has to work harder to achieve the same dilation, which causes more hemorrhaging. This is the death spiral that gives Kyle his two-year window.

## How It Works in Practice

An attacker draws a firearm. Kyle sees the weapon — the NeoCortex array identifies it, calculates barrel length, estimates muzzle velocity from weapon profile, and begins rendering trajectory lines. This happens before the attacker has finished raising the weapon. The red line appears in Kyle's vision, connecting barrel to target.

The attacker's finger moves to the trigger. Kyle's array detects the micro-movements of the hand — the shift in grip pressure, the subtle rotation of the wrist as the index finger curls. The array has catalogued tens of thousands of trigger-pull biomechanics from Dae-jung Seo's training data. It recognizes the initiation of a trigger pull before the trigger has moved a millimeter.

Kyle is already moving.

Not moving fast. Moving early. The temporal dilation gives him subjective seconds to process what is about to happen. The trajectory rendering shows him exactly where the round will go. He steps out of the path — one step, economical, no wasted motion — before the attacker's finger has completed the trigger pull. Before the firing pin has struck the primer. Before the powder has ignited. Before the bullet exists.

The attacker fires. The round passes through the space Kyle occupied a quarter-second ago. To the attacker, it looks like Kyle moved impossibly fast. To Kyle, it felt like he had all the time in the world to take one careful step to the left.

Then the hunger hits.

## The Cost

Kyle does not dodge bullets for free.

Every engagement costs him. A brief firefight — three attackers, maybe eight seconds of real time — might cost him 2,000-3,000 calories and leave him shaking, nauseous, and disoriented for ten to fifteen minutes afterward as his glucose-starved brain compensates. A sustained engagement — a building breach, multiple rooms, continuous threat — can leave him barely functional. He has collapsed after engagements. He has lost consciousness. He has woken up on the floor with Mrs. Chen spooning broth into his mouth.

The degradation is also cumulative. Each use of dilation makes the next use slightly more expensive and slightly less effective. The micro-hemorrhaging builds. The scar tissue accumulates. The two-year clock ticks.

This is why Kyle does not fight unless he has to. This is why his escalation ladder starts with presence — let them see the katana, let them do the math. Most situations end without dilation. The ones that don't end with Kyle eating everything in sight and sleeping for fourteen hours.

## What It Looks Like From the Outside

Witnesses consistently describe three things:

1. **He moved before the shot.** Not during. Not after. Before. Multiple independent accounts describe Kyle beginning his evasive movement while the attacker's weapon was still being raised. This is the most unsettling aspect for witnesses — it implies he knew what was going to happen before it happened.

2. **He only moves enough.** There is no diving, no rolling, no theatrical acrobatics. Kyle shifts by centimeters. A tilt of the torso. A half-step. The minimum distance required to move his body out of the trajectory line. Economy of motion so precise it looks choreographed.

3. **He is visibly wrecked afterward.** Whatever he does costs him something enormous. He sweats. He shakes. His eyes lose focus. He reaches for food within minutes of any engagement. This is the detail that separates Kyle from the movie-hero archetype — he pays for every second of enhanced perception with his own body.

## The Narrative Rule

Kyle does not dodge bullets. He reads the shooter's body language, sees the trajectory before the trigger is pulled, dilates his perception of time to give himself room to move, and steps out of the path. The bullet was never going to hit him — not because he is fast, but because he was already somewhere else by the time it arrived.

This is not superhuman speed. It is superhuman perception married to lethal training and hardware that is eating him alive from the inside.

Every time he uses it, the clock gets shorter.

Every time he doesn't use it, someone might die.

This is the math Kyle lives inside.
